unique_name: Water-Soluble Vitamins (B1, B2, B3, B5, B6, B7, B9, B12, C)
explanation_footer:
Summary

Water-soluble vitamins include the eight B-complex vitamins and vitamin C, which function primarily as enzyme cofactors and antioxidants. Unlike fat-soluble vitamins, they are not stored in significant quantities (vitamin B12, stored in the liver for 2-5 years, is the exception) and must be regularly replenished. Deficiency arises most commonly from alcohol use disorder, malabsorption (eg, celiac disease, Crohn disease, bariatric surgery), strict vegan diet, or drug-nutrient interactions (eg, isoniazid, methotrexate, proton pump inhibitors). Each vitamin produces a distinctive deficiency syndrome that is frequently tested on board exams.

Vitamin B1 (Thiamine)

Biochemistry & Activation

Thiamine is phosphorylated intracellularly to thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), a cofactor for dehydrogenase complexes essential to aerobic glucose metabolism:

Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH): pyruvate → acetyl-CoA (links glycolysis to TCA cycle)

α-Ketoglutarate (α-KG) dehydrogenase: α-KG → succinyl-CoA (TCA cycle)

Transketolase: pentose phosphate pathway; RBC transketolase activity is the laboratory marker for deficiency

Branched-chain α-keto acid (BCAA) dehydrogenase: BCAA catabolism

Deficiency (Beriberi and Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome)

Impaired TPP-dependent enzymes block aerobic metabolism and drive lactic acidosis

Four classic presentations:

Vitamin B1 (Thiamine) Deficiency Syndromes
SyndromeClinical Features
Dry BeriberiSymmetric sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy with motor weakness Slow-onset deficiency
Wet BeriberiHigh-output cardiac failure with dilated cardiomyopathy Peripheral edema and vasodilation Tachycardia Acute-onset deficiency
Wernicke EncephalopathyTriad: confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia (all three present in fewer than 20% of cases) MRI: T2 hyperintensities in mammillary bodies and periaqueductal gray Management: give IV thiamine before glucose (glucose alone can precipitate encephalopathy in thiamine-deficient patients)
Korsakoff SyndromeIrreversible Follows untreated Wernicke Anterograde → retrograde amnesia Confabulation Preserved consciousness

Vitamin B2 (Riboflavin)

Biochemistry & Activation

Riboflavin is the precursor for flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) and flavin mononucleotide (FMN), electron carriers in oxidation-reduction reactions

Key roles include complex II of the electron transport chain (succinate dehydrogenase), fatty acid β-oxidation, and the TCA cycle

Riboflavin also activates vitamins B6 and B9; its deficiency can therefore impair those pathways secondarily

Deficiency

Classic triad:

Angular cheilitis (fissures at corners of the mouth)

Glossitis (erythematous, swollen tongue)

Stomatitis

Additional findings include seborrheic dermatitis and corneal vascularization

Vitamin B3 (Niacin)

Biochemistry & Activation

Niacin is the precursor for NAD+ and NADP+, the most widely used electron carriers in metabolism. NAD+ accepts electrons in catabolism (glycolysis, TCA cycle, β-oxidation); NADP+ drives anabolic reactions (fatty acid synthesis, pentose phosphate pathway)

Tryptophan is a precursor for niacin, so tryptophan depletion or malabsorption can produce pellagra

Deficiency (Pellagra)

Pellagra presents with the 4 Ds:

Dermatitis (photosensitive, hyperpigmented, scaly; casal necklace on the neck)

Diarrhea

Dementia

Death

Causes:

Corn-based diet: corn lacks niacin and is low in tryptophan

Hartnup disease: autosomal recessive disorder caused by defective intestinal and renal transport of neutral amino acids, particularly tryptophan

Carcinoid syndrome: tryptophan diverted to serotonin synthesis, depleting the niacin precursor pool

Isoniazid: inhibition of pyridoxal kinase (reducing B6/PLP), which secondarily impairs the PLP-dependent step in tryptophan → niacin conversion

Pharmacologic Use

At pharmacologic doses, niacin raises HDL cholesterol and lowers triglycerides

Side effects include cutaneous flushing (prostaglandin-mediated; mitigated by aspirin pretreatment), hepatotoxicity, hyperglycemia, and hyperuricemia

Vitamin B5 (Pantothenic Acid)

Biochemistry & Activation

Pantothenic acid is an essential component of coenzyme A (CoA) and the acyl carrier protein (ACP). CoA activates fatty acids as acyl-CoA, is required for acetyl-CoA entry into the TCA cycle, and participates in cholesterol, steroid hormone, and heme synthesis

Deficiency

Isolated deficiency is exceedingly rare

Prolonged total parenteral nutrition without supplementation or severe malnutrition may produce "burning feet" neuropathy, dermatitis, and enteritis

Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine)

Biochemistry & Activation

Pyridoxine is converted to pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), a cofactor for more than 100 enzymes. Board-tested roles:

Transamination, with ALT and AST

ALA synthase: rate-limiting step of heme synthesis (succinyl-CoA + glycine → δ-aminolevulinic acid)

Neurotransmitter synthesis: DOPA decarboxylase (dopamine, norepinephrine), GABA, serotonin

Cystathionine β-synthase: homocysteine → cystathionine; deficiency elevates homocysteine

Deficiency

Impaired ALA synthase produces sideroblastic anemia:

Microcytic, hypochromic RBCs with ring sideroblasts on bone marrow biopsy

Additional findings include peripheral neuropathy, glossitis, and seborrheic dermatitis

Risk factors:

Isoniazid: inhibits pyridoxal kinase, causing functional B6 deficiency and peripheral neuropathy; co-prescribe pyridoxine

Alcohol use disorder: causes sideroblastic anemia; treat with pyridoxine and alcohol cessation

Pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy: neonatal seizures unresponsive to standard anticonvulsants; respond to pharmacologic pyridoxine

Vitamin B7 (Biotin)

Biochemistry & Activation

Biotin is a cofactor for carboxylase enzymes:

Pyruvate carboxylase: pyruvate → oxaloacetate (gluconeogenesis)

Acetyl-CoA carboxylase: acetyl-CoA → malonyl-CoA (rate-limiting step of fatty acid synthesis)

Propionyl-CoA carboxylase: propionyl-CoA → methylmalonyl-CoA (odd-chain fatty acid catabolism)

Methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase: leucine catabolism

Deficiency

Alopecia

Seborrheic dermatitis

Neurologic symptoms (eg, paresthesias, ataxia, seizures)

Caused by prolonged consumption of raw egg whites, which contain avidin, a glycoprotein that binds biotin with high affinity (cooking denatures avidin), or by extended total parenteral nutrition without biotin supplementation

Vitamin B9 (Folate)

Biochemistry & Activation

Dietary folate is reduced to tetrahydrofolate (THF) by dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR). THF donates one-carbon units for:

De novo purine synthesis (adenine, guanine)

Thymidylate synthase: dUMP → dTMP (requires 5,10-methylene-THF); blocked by 5-fluorouracil (5-FU)

Homocysteine → methionine via methionine synthase (requires 5-methyl-THF and B12)

Deficiency

Body stores last approximately 2-4 months. Unlike B12 deficiency, folate deficiency does not cause subacute combined degeneration

Megaloblastic anemia: macrocytic RBCs and hypersegmented neutrophils (≥ 5 lobes) on peripheral smear

Neural tube defects: inadequate folate during the first 3-4 weeks after conception, when neural tube formation and closure occur (completing around day 28), leads to anencephaly, spina bifida, and meningomyelocele. Standard of care is 400 mcg/day periconceptionally

Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin)

Biochemistry & Activation

Dietary cobalamin is released from food protein by gastric acid, bound to intrinsic factor (IF) secreted by gastric parietal cells

Absorbed in the terminal ileum via cubilin receptors

Two active forms serve distinct reactions:

Methylcobalamin: cofactor for methionine synthase (5-methyl-THF + homocysteine → THF + methionine), regenerating THF and creating the folate trap when B12 is absent

Adenosylcobalamin: cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA); deficiency causes accumulation of methylmalonic acid (MMA), the key diagnostic marker

Deficiency

Megaloblastic anemia plus neurologic disease, a combination that folate deficiency alone does not produce

Subacute combined degeneration

Demyelination of the posterior columns (loss of vibration and proprioception) and lateral corticospinal tracts (spastic weakness, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign)

Dementia may develop in advanced disease

Neurologic damage is irreversible if untreated

Pernicious anemia

Autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells leads to loss of intrinsic factor and B12 malabsorption

Diagnosed by anti-intrinsic factor antibodies (specific) or anti-parietal cell antibodies (sensitive)

Associated with autoimmune thyroiditis and type 1 diabetes

Folate trap: Without B12, 5-methyl-THF cannot be converted back to free THF, so folate accumulates in an unusable form and DNA synthesis is impaired even when total folate is adequate. This is why B12 deficiency produces megaloblastic anemia despite normal or elevated serum folate

Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid)

Biochemistry & Functions

Ascorbic acid is a reducing agent and antioxidant with several board-tested roles:

Collagen synthesis: cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase, which hydroxylate proline and lysine in procollagen. Without hydroxylation, the collagen triple helix cannot form, resulting in defective connective tissue

Iron absorption: reduces dietary Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺ at the brush border of duodenal enterocytes; Fe²⁺ is the form absorbed by enterocytes

Antioxidant: scavenges reactive oxygen species; regenerates vitamin E

Dopamine β-hydroxylase: required for norepinephrine synthesis

Deficiency (Scurvy)

All findings reflect defective collagen:

Perifollicular hemorrhages (most specific finding)

Corkscrew hairs (pathognomonic)

Gingival bleeding and swelling, loosening of teeth

Impaired wound healing, poor scar strength

Iron deficiency anemia: loss of Fe³⁺-to-Fe²⁺ conversion in gut

Subperiosteal hemorrhage in children, Trümmerfeld zone on x-ray

Key Takeaways

B1 (thiamine/TPP): cofactor for PDH, α-KG DH, and transketolase. Deficiency produces beriberi and Wernicke encephalopathy. Administer IV thiamine before glucose in patients at risk for thiamine deficiency.

B2 (riboflavin/FAD, FMN): ETC and TCA cofactor. Deficiency produces angular cheilitis, glossitis, and corneal vascularization.

B3 (niacin/NAD+, NADP+): ubiquitous redox carrier. Deficiency produces pellagra (4 Ds). Hartnup disease and carcinoid syndrome are indirect causes via tryptophan depletion. Pharmacologic niacin causes flushing (prostaglandin-mediated; prevent with aspirin).

B5 (pantothenic acid/CoA): fatty acid activation. Deficiency is rare; "burning feet" is the classic finding.

B6 (pyridoxine/PLP): transamination, heme synthesis, neurotransmitters. Deficiency produces sideroblastic anemia (ring sideroblasts on marrow biopsy) and neuropathy. Isoniazid is the classic drug cause.

B7 (biotin): carboxylation reactions. Deficiency produces alopecia, dermatitis, and neurologic symptoms. Raw egg whites (avidin) bind biotin; cooking destroys avidin.

B9 (folate/THF): one-carbon transfer and DNA synthesis. Deficiency produces megaloblastic anemia without neurologic deficits, plus neural tube defects. Supplement 400 mcg/day periconceptionally. Leucovorin rescues methotrexate toxicity.

B12 (cobalamin): absorbed via intrinsic factor in the terminal ileum. Deficiency produces megaloblastic anemia plus subacute combined degeneration. MMA is elevated (distinguishing it from folate deficiency). Folate corrects anemia but not neuropathy, so always replace B12.

Vitamin C (ascorbic acid): collagen hydroxylation, Fe³⁺-to-Fe²⁺ conversion, antioxidant. Deficiency produces scurvy: perifollicular hemorrhages, corkscrew hairs, gingival bleeding.

Elevated homocysteine reflects deficiency of B6, B9, or B12. Elevated MMA is specific for B12 deficiency. Use MMA to distinguish B12 from folate deficiency.

Teaching Cases

Case 1: Wernicke Encephalopathy

A 48-year-old man with chronic alcohol use disorder is brought to the emergency department with acute confusion and inability to walk. Examination shows horizontal nystagmus, bilateral lateral gaze palsy, and truncal ataxia. Diagnosis: Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency; IV thiamine is given before any dextrose. Key teaching: the classic triad is complete in fewer than 20% of cases, so treat empirically when deficiency is suspected.

Case 2: Pellagra in Hartnup Disease

A 4-year-old girl presents with episodic watery diarrhea, a scaly photosensitive rash, and intermittent ataxia. Laboratory studies confirm impaired intestinal absorption of neutral amino acids including tryptophan. Diagnosis: Hartnup disease, in which tryptophan malabsorption depletes the precursor pool for niacin synthesis, producing pellagra. Key teaching: any condition limiting tryptophan availability can cause pellagra even without a niacin-deficient diet.

Case 3: B12 Deficiency After Bariatric Surgery

A 54-year-old woman, 2 years after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, presents with bilateral foot numbness, decreased vibration sense, hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, MCV 105 fL, and hypersegmented neutrophils. Serum B12 is low; MMA and homocysteine are elevated. Diagnosis: vitamin B12 deficiency from reduced gastric acid and bypass of proximal absorptive sites. Key teaching: elevated MMA confirms B12 (not folate) deficiency; folate alone corrects anemia but allows neuropathy to progress.
